# Introduction
<!--  Situation  --> 
The release of 
Toronto's *Big Move* in 2008 [@Salsberg:2010aa] 
provides an early example of the 'mobility hub' concept, 
in the context of regional transport and landuse planning. 
More recently, 
the ``Shared Mobility Hub" idea has been introduced, 
wherein 
"...emphasis is given on shared mobility options such as bikes, scooters and cars(, while c)onnection with public transport (transit) is desirable but not necessary" [@Roukouni:2023aa]. 
Shared *electric* mobility hubs, 
sometimes called eHUBs [@Bosehans:2023aa], 
add the possibility of on-site recharging 
of micro-mobility vehicles (as well as shared e-cars). 
Along such lines, 
four shared e-mobility hubs have recently been implemented in 
Ireland 
as part of the Electric shaRed mOBilityhUbS Trial (ROBUST) project [@ROBUST:2025aa].
Each hub includes 
e-bikes, 
e-cargo bikes, 
and shared electric cars 
as part of the ‘base’ offering, 
as well as power infrastructure to support recharging of these vehicles, 
and other potential future uses [@Atlantic-Technological-University:2025ab, @Atlantic-Technological-University:2025aa, @Waterford-City-and-County-Council:2025aa]. 


<!--  Problem  -->
Shared micromobility, 
including dockless e-bike and e-scooter systems, 
have variously faced challenges, including: 
poor user behaviour with respect to parking; 
a need for workers to re-position vehicles and replace batteries; 
poor build quality of many such vehicles; 
market distortion, including related to 
large fleets in central areas;
and the risk of fires when battery recharging is done using non-bespoke or appropriately designed facilities (e.g. in gig-workers' houses)(see @Zhang:2022aa, @Meigs:2023aa, @Ferguson:2025aa and others).
In contrast, 
at the ROBUST hubs 
there is a dedicated charging 
and parking space for each micro-mobility vehicle, 
which has to be returned to the same hub from which it was hired 
(i.e. A-to-A trips only). 
This may provide 
operational advantages (minimal staffing), 
but also for a more community-based 
service profile 
(with hubs potentially located in small towns 
or outside of city centres) 
so as to help towards 
providing for last-mile and 
and more occasional trips 
that cannot be easily accomplished 
on foot, 
personal bicycle 
or by transit. 
A nearby eHUB might also help 
communities transition to 
electric cars, 
without the large
capital expense 
involved in purchasing a private e-car. 

<!--  Question  --> 
As of yet, 
however, 
not much is known about 
eHUBS with on-site recharging of micro-mobility vehicles. 
It is unclear how the return-to-origin (A-to-A) 
restriction might impact on users and useability/practicality.   
Nor is it clear what potential hub offerings 
might better meet community needs (including through expansion). 
There also appears to be only limited understandings about 
how best to communicate information about such a hub and how to use it. 

<!--  Answer  --> 
Research understandings about eHUBs 
appear to be at an early stage, 
for which many authors^[See, for example, @Bonoma:1984aa, @Benbasat:1987aa, @Eisenhardt:1989aa, @Meredith:1993aa, @ Cavaye:1996aa, @Darke:1998aa, @Stuart:2002aa, @Voss:2002aa and @Yin:2018ab.] 
suggest adopting an exploratory case research approach. 
Industrial-design-based approaches, 
including those well suited to transport research 
^[See @Coxon:2018aa, @Coxon:2021ab, @Gaitan:2021aa, @Napper:2021aa, @Pink:2021aa, @UK-Design-Council:0aa and others.], 
such variously adopting iterative, 
co-design and participatory,
and creative 
processes. 
As such, this paper reports the findings from 
workshops with 
members of the public 
and project stakeholders 
held in Letterkenny, Galway and Waterford 
to explore 
attitudes, needs and ideas 
as to how the ‘base’ shared e-mobility hub might be leveraged 
and enhanced so as to better meet each community’s transport and other needs. 
The cross-case comparisons 
reported in this paper 
might provide policy-makers, 
practitioners and researchers 
further insights into the types of offerings that might be provided 
at shared e-mobility hubs and other transport facilities 
in a variety of contexts (small town, secondary town centre, suburban locations etc.) 
so as to enhance sustainable mobility and community outcomes 
in future such transport facility developments.

# Background and context

SEAMLESS


Overall, therefore, this exploratory study focuses on three questions that appear especially relevant to eHUBs where all vehilces (including micro-mobility vehicles) have their own dedicated parking space and charging infrastructure. Taking the ROBUST hubs as initially implemented as a 'base scenario', the study examines:

- How a return-to-origin (A-to-A) restriction minght impact on users and useability? 
- How hub offerings might better meet community needs (including through expansion)?
- How information about a hub and how to use it be effectively communicated? 


# Methodology

## Study design

This study adopts a case-research design, 
based around the four hubs in the Electric shaRed mOBilityhUbS Trial (ROBUST) project.
Case studies can be particularly useful for exploratory research, 
where the researchers do not have control over events 
(limiting the feasibility of case-control experiments), 
and where questions relate to 'how' or 'why'. 
This contrasts to quantitative approaches 
that are often based around having 
large, 
random 
and independent samples, 
and a search for statistically significant answers 
to 'how many' or 'what' types of questions. 
Instead, case research typically involves 
only a small number of individual units, 
which can facilitate greater depth of engagement 
with each 
and its context (@Yin:2018ab and others). 

Some common misunderstandings about case-based methods, 
however, 
relate to the sampling frame. 
The methodological literature 
emphasises inclusion of cases 
based being 
critical, leading or insightful, 
or to allow for replication or the examination of polar opposites. 
The "duality criterion" is also a consideration, 
in that case researchers 
need to be at the same time: 
grounded in the context of each case, 
allowing phenomenon to be examined in great depth; 
yet also seeking generalisation 
such that findings can be reasonably extrapolated 
to be apply to other circumstances (beyond the studied cases)
(@Benbasat:1987aa, @Bonoma:1984aa, @Darke:1998aa, @Meredith:1998aa, @Stuart:2002aa, @Denscombe:2007aa, @Ketokivi:2014aa, @Yin:2018ab and others)

Here the case selection is largely forced 
(i.e. for non-theoretical reasons) 
due to the circumstances of the larger ROBUST project 
and conditions of the research funding. 
However, this also represents a unique opportunity, 
in that the four implemented hubs exist 
because of this funding 
and there are no known other locations 
with hubs 
with a dedicated 
on-site parking and charging space 
for each (*micro-mobility*) vehicle. 
Dedicated parking on a one-to-one basis
is common in car and other large vehicle sharing, 
but contrasts to the typical 
shared micro-mobility systems 
where there is usually more parking space(s) than vehicles. 
As such, the ROBUST trial 
represents a unique opportunity for the 
researchers 
to gain access to stakeholders or community attitudes 
related to a return-to-origin (A-to-A) model of 
shared micromobility.   


## Context of the Electric shaRed mOBilityhUbS Trial (ROBUST) project

The Electric shaRed mOBility hUbS Trial (ROBUST) project involves four sites. Table \@ref(hub_details) provides brief summary of the characteristics of the surrounds of each hub^[Further details, including site photos, are available at \url{https://james-reynolds.github.io/ROBUST_Electric_shaRed_mOBility_hUbS_Trial_website/}.]. 
'Initial offers' of 
four electric bikes (e-bikes), 
one electric cargo bike (e-cargobike) and two electric cars (e-cars) 
were implemented during 2025 and 2026. 
These 'initial offers' were largely designed and implemented by engineers,
planners and other technical specialists to meet the basic needs and
functionality requirements associated 
with parking and charging the seven vehicles at each site. 
Location selection was also somewhat constrained by 
outside factors, 
such as obtaining permissions from local authorities, 
power supply and space requirements, 
and other issues. 
However, the four sites 
represent a 
range of contexts, 
including a smaller town (Letterkenny), 
near a secondary centre in a larger city (Westside, Galway), 
the "Ballybricken Green" and surrounding shopping precint (Waterford), 
and near a major suburban shopping centre (Dundrum, Dublin), 
which may help towards 
cross-case comparison and generalisation 
in this exploratory case study.

E-cars were managed by Enterprise, 
as part of their 'Car Club' offering, 
necessitating users to pay a membership fee^[5 Euros a month for occasional users, or 40 Euros for a whole year]
along with hourly and kilometre charges 
that vary based on location and vehicle type. 
A one-year free membership 
and 10 Euro driving credit was offered 
through a promotional code 
to new users 
in the months immediately after the launch of each hub. 

E-bikes and e-cargobikes were provided by MOBY, 
and managed by ESB. 
The initial pricing was set based on a start fee (1 Euro), 
and an hourly charge (5 Euros, charged for each hour or part thereof). 
A promotional code was likewise offered 
in the months immediately after the launch of each hub, 
providing users with a single free trial ride of up to 3 hours duration.  
However, users needed to have 
a minimum wallet balance of 10 Euros 
within the ESB eHub app^[See \url{https://apps.apple.com/us/app/esb-ehub/id1612495746} or \url{https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sharebike.android.esb&hl=en_IE}] 
for users to be able to rent the e-bikes or e-cargobikes.
Usage of the e-cars 
similarly required the use of a mobile phone app, 
being the standard Enterprise Car Club offering.
A further "ROBUST Mobility Hubs" app was also 
available^[\url{https://apps.apple.com/ie/app/robust-mobility-hubs/id6755043620}], 
although due to technical constraints 
this only directed new users to an online survey, 
and then on to the Enterprise and ESB apps 
for the vehicle hire functionality. 
Various posters, leaflets, online and social media posts
and other advertising material 
was distributed around the time of each hub launch. 
The hub launches also received some media attention 
as well as posts on various stakeholder and other institutional webpages ^[e.g. @Atlantic-Technological-University:2025ab, @Atlantic-Technological-University:2025aa, @Waterford-City-and-County-Council:2025aa, 
@ESB:0aa, and @Kelleher:2025aa]

## Processes and instruments

The case-based research 
reported in this paper 
occurred with the 12-month period 
between the launch of the 
Waterford and Dublin hubs^[End 
of October 2025 to beginning of November 2026.]. 
This activity included two components 
specifically based around human participants: 
(1) behaviour nudging and 
(2) co-design workshops; 
for which ethics approval was obtained,^[Part of ATU Research Ethics application UREC_ATU_2026_347, approval granted May 27, 2026. A separate research ethics approval from Trinity College Dublin (REAMSs No 4432, approved June 16, 2025, covered other components of the ROBUST project involving human participants (i.e. collection of data about users and usage).], 
as well activities undertaken by the ROBUST team and partner organisations. 
These two components 
were largerly aligned with ROBUST's aims^[For each hub 
"to serve as an incubator, accelerating the uptake of electric mobility options by allowing interacting with future mobility technologies and removing barriers through participatory research (and with v)arious stakeholders...engaged in the process of hub evolution through stakeholder workshops and co-creation workshops" [@ROBUST:2025aa]]. 

A strength of case-research approaches 
is  that they allow for drift [@Benbasat:1987aa, @Bonoma:1984aa, @Voss:2002aa], which might allow for iteration, 
and adjustment to respond to 
the changed circumstances 
that might occur 
when researchers do not have full control of events. 
As discussed in later sections, 
such 'drift' was encountered during the ROBUST project, 
primarily related to the 
limits of available funding for research activity 
being reached. 
The ROBUST project received considerably less funding than had been applied for, yet the number of included hubs (4) was not reduced. 
Hence the originally envisaged hub incubation was abandoned, while the behaviour nudging and co-design workshop programs were curtailed. 
Other challenges related to: 
a lack of project control over site selection^[Largely set 
by institutional and political stakeholders.];
vehicle availability, management and maintenance; and 
technological issues, including related to app functionality and data sharing. 
As such, 
the next two subsections 
briefly outline the two components 
of the research for which ethics approval was received 
(as these remained, for obvious reasons, within relatively tight boundaries). 
The 'drift' in other parts of the case research and context, 
and the researchers' adjustments,
however, 
are described linearly 
through time along with the presentation of results later in the paper. 


### Behaviour nudging

Development of the behaviour nudging component 
drew on background context 
from travel behaviour, 
transport marketing, 
and education and encouragement programs, 
such as the "TravelSmart", "IndiMark" and "TravelBlending approaches 
(see @AMPT:1998aa, @brog1998marketing, 
@Giuliano:2005aa, @james2017travelsmart 
and others). 
It was unclear if such tailored marking approaches, 
long used in the contexts of transit 
and non-motorised travel, 
might be effective in 
encouraging the use of eHUBs. 
As such, 
the behaviour-nudging component 
of the research envisaged 
mail-out and/or in-person delivery 
of individualized material to nearby addresses, 
posters and leaflets, 
social media engagement 
and the recruitment of 'local heroes' 
for each hub. 
This was also seen as an avenue for 
informal discussion between the researchers and community members 
(especially during in-person delivery of materials) 
as a way to gain understandings about 
community attitudes to the hubs, 
initial offers and
the potential of eHUBS. 

### Co-design workshops
The ROBUST research aims 
and the gaps in understandings discussed earlier in this paper
also relate to: participatory research; 
eHUB design and how offerings might better meet community needs; and
information provision to users. 
Initial development of this component of the research 
was informed by the background context of 
applying industrial design approaches 
to challenges in transportation. 
@Coxon:2018aa, @Pink:2021aa, @Napper:2021aa, and @Gaitan:2021aa 
provide examples of this approach, 
which is often based around the UK Design Council's 
Double Diamond Framework for Innovation [@UK-Design-Council:0aa].  
This is iterative, 
but involves switching between divergent and convergent approaches 
across four steps.  
In the context of the ROBUST hubs, 
these were conceptualised as involving
*discovering* the initial offer's 
strengths, weaknesses and opportunities for improvement; 
*defining* these as problems to be addressed; 
*developing* options; 
and *delivering* an improvement on the implemented 
'initial offer' that might form a basis for future mobility hubs.  

## Participants and materials

### Researchers 
This paper picks up the case study narrative after the launch 
of the Galway, Letterkenny and Waterford hubs. 
However, by then ROBUST project had 
already been underway for two years, 
with the focus on infrastructure implementation. 
Over that time there had been some changes to 
research personnel^[As originally proposed, 
ROBUST was led by Trinity College Dublin (TCD), 
involving five staff (The Principal Investigator (Author 7), 
the original Project Manager (Author 6) and three others.
Two staff at Atlantic Technological University (ATU) 
were also involved, 
one at the Sligo and the other at the Galway campus.  
It had been anticipated that 
two PhD students based at ATU would be recruited 
to the project.],
the aforementioned reduction in funding, 
and other changes. 
These led to the researchers participating in the 
case studies being: 

- Author 1: a full-time two-year post-doctoral researcher at ATU who was variously: travelling around the hub locations, but based mostly out of Galway for September and October 2025; then stuck back in Australia until late May (earlier flights cancelled by the US-Iran war); and then based at the Sligo campus;
- Author 2: a part-time research assistant on a 7-month-long contract at ATU;
- Author 3: an academic at the ATU Galway campus, but with no time formally allocated to ROBUST; 
- Author 4: an academic at the ATU Sligo campus, who likewise had no time formally allocated to the project; 
- Author 5: the Project Manager at TCD who had been recruited after the original Project Manager and main author of the proposal (Author 6) moved to the UK; and 
- Author 7: the Principal Investigator. 

Within ATU there was only limited budgetary allocations 
for travel or other expenses 
(in the order of 6,000 Euros). 
The development of behaviour nudging and co-design materials 
therefore needed to be undertaken primarily using 
open source and free software 
and data sources. 
Author 1 had some previous experience with using 
the R programing language for geospatial analysis, 
and so the case research relied on 
Open Street Maps (OSM) datasets 
and various software packages including 
sf [@R-sf], 
osmdata [@osmdata2017] and
the tufte styles for document presentation [@R-tufte]. 

Inputs to the co-design research activities also came from the 
mobilityHubTools *R package*, 
This had been developed as part of the 
ROBUST research 
based on case studies of UK mobility hub 
informational signage, 
and provides basic functionality to produce totem sign layouts 
in three styles^[As per mobility hubs in (1) Bristol and (2) 
Brimingham, and as a (3) synthesis style.] 
for any location, using OSM datasets. 
The initial development of this tool 
has been reported elsewhere (in @Reynolds:2026aa), 
but provided the method of generating 
information displays mock-ups 
for the Galway, Letterkenny and Waterford hubs 
as input material for discussions during the co-design workshops, 
and as a continuance and further iteration 
of that earlier reported research.  

### Project partners

Similarly to the research team, 
there had been some changes to involvement 
amongst the industry partners since the time 
of the original ROBUST proposal^[The proposal identified involvement from staff at ESB (2) and Enterprise (5).]. 
In part this is due to some roles being more focused towards 
hub implementation, and so having contracts that implemented.

## A 'home' institution for each hub?

Maybe there is a need for a 'front desk' nearby each mobility hub that has responsibility to assist users, help with new user sign up, day-to-day security and operational management (including checking that everything is working), 
and being the first port of call for assistance. 


Basing mobility hubs at:
- service stations (24hr staffing?)
- railway and bus stations
- hotels, camp sites and other accommodation
- bike shopes and rental places
